posts.title: Choosing your first drivetrain
posts.author: Reyansh
posts.body:
Mecanum, tank or swerve? For most rookie teams, a mecanum drivetrain built from a kit chassis is the best balance of speed, agility and simplicity.

If the game rewards lining up sideways with targets, mecanum wins. If you need to push, tank drive with traction wheels is stronger.

Whatever you pick: keep the frame square, belt tension consistent and the battery low and centered.

posts.title: Odometry pods in a weekend
posts.author: Reyansh
posts.body:
Dead-wheel odometry tells your autonomous exactly where the robot is.

1. Mount two parallel pods and one perpendicular pod, spring-loaded onto the mat.
2. Convert encoder ticks to inches using wheel diameter and ticks per revolution.
3. Use a library like Road Runner or Pedro Pathing to turn readings into a pose and follow paths.

Tune by pushing the robot a measured distance and comparing.

posts.title: Wiring that never fails at competition
posts.author: Reyansh
posts.body:
Most robot failures at events are electrical.

Use strain relief on every connector, label both ends of every cable and keep motor and sensor wires apart.

Before each match: battery voltage, a tug on each connector and a quick motor test.

posts.title: Build a soft robot gripper in one weekend
posts.author: Neodymium Zenith
posts.body:
Rigid robots grip with motors and gears. Soft robots grip with air. Pump air into a silicone finger with tiny chambers on one side and a stiff layer on the other, and it curls like a real finger. It's gentle enough to pick up an egg or a strawberry. Here's how to build one in a weekend.

THE IDEA
The finger has two layers. The top layer is full of small air chambers (a "PneuNet"). The bottom layer has paper or fabric inside it, so it can bend but not stretch. When the chambers inflate they push against each other, the bottom can't stretch, and the finger curls.

SATURDAY MORNING — Molds (2–3 hours)
Print the two mold halves: the top mold with chamber ribs and a flat bottom mold. Free mold files are on the [Soft Robotics Toolkit](https://softroboticstoolkit.com/) and the [Science Buddies soft gripper project](https://www.sciencebuddies.org/science-fair-projects/project_ideas/Robotics_p020.shtml). No printer? Build the mold from LEGO bricks on a flat baseplate.
Spray every surface with mold release and let it dry.

SATURDAY AFTERNOON — Cast the top layer (30 min work, 4 hours curing)
1. Put on gloves. Mix Ecoflex 00-30 Part A and Part B 1:1 by weight on a digital scale. Stir slowly for 3 minutes, scraping the sides and bottom.
2. Pour slowly into the top mold from one corner, so air bubbles escape. Tap the mold on the table for a minute.
3. Leave it to cure for at least 4 hours at room temperature.

SATURDAY EVENING — Cast the bottom layer
1. Pour a thin layer (2–3 mm) of fresh Ecoflex into the flat mold.
2. Lay a strip of printer paper or thin fabric on top. This is the layer that doesn't stretch.
3. Pour a little more silicone over it. Leave it overnight.

SUNDAY MORNING — Join and seal
1. Peel both layers out of the molds.
2. Brush a thin coat of fresh Ecoflex onto the bottom layer and press the top layer (chambers facing down) onto it. Don't let silicone flow into the chambers.
3. When it's cured, insert the silicone tube into the end chamber and seal around it with Sil-Poxy.

SUNDAY MIDDAY — First test
Attach a hand pump or a large syringe and squeeze gently. The finger should curl. Submerge it in water and inflate: bubbles show any leak. Dab on silicone and let it cure.
Go slowly. Over-inflating makes a balloon bulge and then a pop.

SUNDAY AFTERNOON — Make it robotic
Swap the hand pump for a 12V mini air pump and a solenoid valve, both switched by an Arduino through a relay or MOSFET module. Pump on and valve closed to grip; pump off and valve open to release. Mount three or four fingers on a 3D-printed hub for a full gripper.

WHAT YOU'LL BUY (search these on Amazon)
Silicone and casting: Smooth-On Ecoflex 00-30 trial unit; silicone mold release spray; [Sil-Poxy adhesive](https://link.amazon/B043ylB9m); digital scale (0.1 g); mixing cups and stir sticks; [nitrile gloves](https://link.amazon/B0dZtPZru); [PLA filament](https://link.amazon/B0cNZsoU7) or LEGO bricks.
Air and plumbing: 1/8" silicone tubing; 1/8" barbed connectors and Y-splitters; 60 mL Luer-lock syringes or a squeeze-bulb pump.
Electronics: Arduino Uno; 12V mini air pump; 12V mini solenoid air valve; relay or MOSFET module; 12V 2A power supply; breadboard and jumper wires.

TIPS
- Work in a ventilated room and wear safety glasses when testing pressure.
- Mix by weight, not by eye. A wrong mix never fully cures.
- Silicone only bonds well to silicone, so join layers with fresh silicone, not superglue.
- Expect your first finger to leak. The second one is always better.

notes.author: Neodymium Zenith
notes.text:
We built a soft robot gripper in a weekend: silicone fingers that curl when you pump in air. Gentle enough to pick up an egg.

Sat: 3D print molds, cast Ecoflex
Sun: seal, leak-test, add an Arduino + mini pump

notes.author: Neodymium Zenith
notes.text:
Soft robots don't have hard joints or gears. They're made of rubbery materials like silicone and move by pumping in air, so they bend, squeeze and grip like an octopus arm.

That makes them safe around people and gentle enough to pick a strawberry.
